verdicts.text: The post was updated in 2025-03-05 and was originally published 2024-09-25.

verdicts.text: With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's CDK comparison page backs this up: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." This matches the well-known way CDK synthesizes templates, but the source is a pulumi.com page, not AWS docs, so it counts as corroboration only.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim is accurate for CDK. For plain CloudFormation it reads loosely: hand-written CFN templates are the intermediate format themselves, not a code generator that produces one.

verdicts.text: Table-of-contents anchor links point to /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ sections, which match the headings in the post.
verdicts.evidence: All six TOC fragments (L76-81) match actual H2 headings in the post: "## The Beginnings of SST" (L83), "## CDK and CloudFormation Limitations" (L89), "## A Provider-agnostic Solution: Discovering Pulumi" (L110), "## Transitioning to Pulumi" (L120), "## The Benefits of Pulumi" (L128), "## The Future of SST with Pulumi" (L162). The path /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ is listed in the front matter `aliases` (L60), so it redirects to this post.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The TOC links go through the old alias URL, not the canonical /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ or bare #fragments. That means an extra redirect, and #fragments may get dropped if the alias uses a meta-refresh redirect. Bare anchors (#the-beginnings-of-sst) would be more robust.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own blog confirms that earlier SST versions ran on CDK: "We are working on a new version of SST that's not based on CDK." A second write-up says "the first two versions of SST were basically the wrappers and enhancers of AWS CDK." It's well known that AWS CDK supports TypeScript and Python, along with Java, C# and Go.
verdicts.intuition_flag: SST v2 itself only let you write TypeScript/JavaScript. The sentence credits TS/Python support to CDK, which is correct, but readers could take it to mean SST supported Python.

verdicts.text: With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: This is standard AWS CDK behavior, and Pulumi's CDK comparison page backs it up: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." One small wording issue: CloudFormation doesn't generate code itself. Its templates are the intermediate format that CDK produces, which is how the sentence reads in context.
verdicts.framing_note: The only corroboration is another pulumi.com page, backed by general knowledge of `cdk synth` behavior; I didn't fetch an AWS page to confirm it directly.

verdicts.text: Pulumi docs pages exist at /docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation and /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/#what-is-aws-cdk.
verdicts.evidence: Both pages are in the repo and have the headings the anchors point to: cloudformation.md L37 "## What is AWS CloudFormation?" and aws-cdk.md L35 "## What is AWS CDK?". Hugo turns these headings into the anchors #what-is-aws-cloudformation and #what-is-aws-cdk.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports extensibility via custom providers and dynamic components (dynamic providers).
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's docs describe dynamic providers built on the `pulumi.dynamic.ResourceProvider` interface. They also say dynamic providers "are lighter weight than custom providers" and point to bridged or native providers for more complex APIs, so both extension mechanisms exist.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi calls these "dynamic providers" (or dynamic resource providers), not "dynamic components"; the claim's parenthetical clarifies, but the post's wording could be tightened.

verdicts.text: Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; it treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says the CLI launches the language host to execute the program directly. As the program runs, it sends resource registrations to the engine, and no template file sits in between: "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program. When the first ... object is constructed, the language host sends a _resource registration_ request to the deployment engine and then continues executing the program."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim contrasts Pulumi with CDK's generated CloudFormation templates. The guide supports that: the program runs during `pulumi up` and registers resources with the engine as it goes. Nothing in it says Pulumi first writes out a template.

verdicts.text: A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't find an independent source for this quote. The only place it appears is the blog post under review (pulumi.com/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/), and that post can't verify itself. The job title does check out: the PulumiUP 2024 page lists "Dax Raad (Founding Engineer, SST)" as the speaker of the "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST" talk, so the quote probably comes from that talk, but I couldn't find a transcript to confirm the wording.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code\" Pulumi"; top results didn't address the claim. Title corroboration: https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.framing_note: The quote is attributed to a role, not a published document, and no primary source (talk transcript or case study) turned up.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording ("intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things...") reads like marketing paraphrase. Check it against the PulumiUP 2024 SST talk recording before publishing it as a verbatim quote.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi Insights product page provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.
verdicts.evidence: /product/pulumi-insights/ still resolves, but only as an alias that redirects to the Discovery & governance page. That page is about compliance, policy, and searching cloud resources, not debugging deployments. The closest it gets is "Pulumi discovers all resources, including those created outside infrastructure-as-code, providing complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting."
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the target page offers 'visibility for governance and troubleshooting' of cloud resources and compliance. The blog links it as 'improved visibility and debugging capabilities' into the deployment process, which it credits to the code being the same as the deployment code (L136, L169).
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link points to a retired Insights URL. The Pulumi Insights branding has been folded into Discovery & governance, so the anchor text no longer describes where the link lands.

verdicts.text: With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployments.
verdicts.evidence: SST's "Moving away from CDK" post says custom logic that can't be expressed in CloudFormation needs a Custom Resource, "a Lambda function that can execute as a part of the deployment process." It adds that "the CDK community (and us included) need to rely on this for basically anything that isn't supported."
verdicts.framing_note: SST's post describes Custom Resources (Lambda functions) as an escape hatch, calls them a "workaround," and says SST relied on them for anything unsupported. The blog's word "hacky" is its own paraphrase, but SST's post backs up the substance.

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
verdicts.evidence: The languages docs say "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL," and the meta description names AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Kubernetes as targets. The claim's four languages are a correct subset of that list, not an exhaustive one. I didn't check the on-premises part directly, but it's consistent with Pulumi's Kubernetes and other self-hosted providers.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim lists 4 of the 8 supported languages. It doesn't say "only", so it isn't false, though it does undersell (Java, YAML and HCL are left out).

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows such as faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and granular control.
verdicts.evidence: The claim gets the page wrong. L168 says the SST team "can create more advanced deployment workflows that address the specific needs of application developers, such as faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control". That describes what SST plans to build, not something Pulumi Cloud Deployments offers today. The link only points to the Deployments docs, so there is no checkable statement about Pulumi's features here.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the page says SST "can create more advanced deployment workflows ... such as faster deployment times, better rollback"; the claim turns that into "Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides" those things.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The anchor text links to Pulumi Deployments docs, and a reader could take that to mean Deployments has rollback features. It may be worth rewording the line so it doesn't suggest that.

verdicts.text: SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure.

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for SST's new engine for deploying SST applications, deploying constructs/components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: SST's January 2024 post does say "Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3." But SST's August 2024 v3 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3." So the facts are right (Ion was the code name, it swapped CDK/CFN for Pulumi, and it became v3), but the future tense is two years out of date. SST's own post also says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source's Jan 2024 roadmap statement ("will be released as SST v3") is published as current status, but SST says Ion shipped as v3 in Aug 2024. The claim also leaves out SST's note that components are "defined using Terraform providers".
verdicts.intuition_flag: Future-tense roadmap language in a post being refreshed in 2026. Pulumi docs PR #21673 already rewrites this FAQ because it was stale.

verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
verdicts.evidence: SST's Jan 2024 post said "Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3," and that happened. SST's Aug 20, 2024 v3 post says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3." The fact is right, but the future tense is out of date.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source called it a future plan in Jan 2024; the release happened Aug 20, 2024. Suggested fix: "Ion has since been released as SST v3 (August 2024)."
verdicts.intuition_flag: This future-tense sentence repeats a Jan 2024 statement in a post being edited in 2026, more than two years after v3 shipped.

verdicts.text: SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console; the Console is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: SST's pricing update post says "You don't need the Console to use SST" and "You can continue using the Console as a part of the free tier." SST's Console docs describe a free tier of 350 active resources or fewer, with a charge of $0.086 per resource above that. SST's pages confirm the Console is optional, paid, and has a free tier. I didn't find an SST statement that the Console is its *primary* source of revenue, so that part is inferred: the Console is the only paid SST product the search turned up.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim that the Console is optional and has a free tier matches SST's pages exactly. "Makes money primarily through" is my inference from the Console being SST's paid product; SST doesn't say it in words.

verdicts.evidence: This is the blog post's own frontmatter publication date. It is metadata the author sets for the post, not a factual assertion that can be checked against an outside source.

verdicts.text: We wrote up what "built on the Pulumi engine" actually means mechanically, why a framework would rather embed an engine than write one, and where SST stands today (still shipping, team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode).

The same team now also builds opencode: "OpenCode is a terminal-based AI coding agent built by the team behind SST (now Anomaly)." The "we wrote up" part describes the post itself and isn't something that can be checked.

verdicts.text: SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.

One caveat: `home` can be "aws" or "cloudflare". The S3 wording fits the AWS home case; a Cloudflare home stores state in Cloudflare instead.

verdicts.framing_note: The source covers any `home` provider ("aws" and "cloudflare" are supported). The claim states only the AWS/S3 case.

verdicts.text: The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine architecture.

The SST v3 launch post (Aug 2024) says the new engine "would use Pulumi and Terraform". So SST has said this more than once, in its own docs and blog.

verdicts.text: `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say the sst.config.ts run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components", and that "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine." Together these support the pipeline: config, then SST components, then Pulumi resources.
verdicts.framing_note: The SST docs describe components built on the Pulumi engine. "Compile into Pulumi resource declarations" is the claim's own loose wording: SST components are Pulumi component resources, not a separate compile step.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine diffs desired versus actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/pulumi's pkg/resource/deploy package handles "planning and executing resource deployments" and "coordinating the execution and parallelism of the underlying operations", and contains step_generator.go (diffs desired against prior state) and step_executor.go (runs the ordered steps). That matches the claim's general description. One nuance: by default the engine diffs against the last recorded state in the checkpoint, not live cloud state, unless you run a refresh.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "actual state" is loose: Pulumi diffs against recorded state (the checkpoint), not live infrastructure, unless you refresh.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations; Pulumi's Terraform bridge translates each resource into cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That backs the bridge's role in general. The pre-fetched body is truncated, so it doesn't cover the engine diff/graph details or the exact "cloud API calls" mechanism.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says 'bridges Terraform providers into Pulumi'; the claim simplifies this to 'translates each resource into cloud API calls'. In practice the bridged Terraform provider makes the API calls, not the bridge itself, but the simplification is acceptable for a blog.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs in SST.
verdicts.evidence: SST's platform/package.json depends on "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0" plus @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/docker-build and @pulumiverse/vercel, so SST provisions through the Pulumi engine and its providers. Dependency graphing, preview/diff and state tracking are standard jobs of the Pulumi engine. I couldn't find an SST source file that confirms each of those four functions separately.
verdicts.framing_note: This line sums up what the Pulumi engine does, based on the SST quotes earlier in the post. SST keeps state in its own S3 bucket (L75), but the Pulumi engine still does the state tracking, so the two lines don't conflict.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "hundreds of provider APIs" is loose wording. SST itself says "more than 150 other providers" (L45).

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: AWS said CloudFormation already covered "over 900 resource types" in April 2022. A third-party catalog now lists "1613 AWS CloudFormation resource types across 280 services." So "hundreds" holds as a lower bound, though the real count is over a thousand.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds" understates it: AWS now has more than 1,000 resource types (about 1,600 in CloudFormation). The author may want to say "over a thousand".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated `pulumi login` CLI reference documents self-managed backends that need no Pulumi Cloud account: "To manage state yourself, pass the URL of a supported storage backend instead" (file://, s3://, gs://, azblob://, postgres://), and "-l, --local   Use Pulumi in local-only mode".
verdicts.intuition_flag: The phrase "any Pulumi-hosted service" is absolute. By default, provider plugins download from get.pulumi.com, and the CLI checks for updates. Both can be avoided (plugins installed ahead of time, PULUMI_SKIP_UPDATE_CHECK), but the author may want to add a qualifier.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: The cited repo describes itself as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That backs up the basic fact that the bridge brings Terraform providers into Pulumi. Nothing in the fetched page says it was built "specifically to let projects like SST" do this.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says 'A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', but the claim adds a purpose it doesn't state, 'built specifically to let projects like SST reuse...'
verdicts.intuition_flag: The bridge was mainly built so Pulumi could offer its own bridged providers (aws, gcp, etc.), not for third-party frameworks like SST. The word "specifically" is probably wrong.

verdicts.text: A blog post exists at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ titled 'Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi'; docs page /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exists.
verdicts.evidence: content/blog/any-terraform-provider/index.md exists with title: "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi". content/docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers.md exists (title "Use Terraform Providers"), so /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ resolves.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools in the same embedded way.
verdicts.evidence: The cited docs page says Automation API is "a strongly typed SDK, so you can drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell." That supports the idea of embedding Pulumi programs in your own tools. The same page also notes that "Automation API drives the Pulumi CLI under the hood," so the CLI still has to be available when the program runs.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application' and the claim says 'embedding Pulumi programs inside teams' own tools'. These are paraphrases of the same idea.

verdicts.text: Nitric, Defang, and SST expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
verdicts.evidence: SST: Atomic Object says "SST uses Pulumi's AWS provider and leverages Pulumi's engine," and fireup.pro says Ion "uses Pulumi as the deployment runtime and Terraform providers under the hood." Nitric's FAQ says its framework and CLI "use the Pulumi Go Providers." Defang ships Pulumi providers (pulumi-defang) that deploy with Pulumi. That supports the main claim that all three put opinionated interfaces on top of Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: Sources say each tool is built on Pulumi. The "provider bridge underneath" detail is confirmed directly only for SST (Terraform providers). For Nitric and Defang it holds only indirectly, through bridged providers such as pulumi-aws.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Nitric's docs say its providers are "built using Terraform or Pulumi," so Nitric doesn't depend on Pulumi alone. The claim could note that Nitric also has Terraform-based providers.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
verdicts.evidence: The claim that "most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code" is an assertion about how SST's user base behaves, and the post gives no source for it. Neither Pulumi source code nor public docs measure what share of SST users write raw Pulumi. The sources quoted on L61 only say that SST "lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs," which says nothing about how many users do.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most" users is a guess with no data behind it; consider softening it to "SST users don't need to write Pulumi code."

verdicts.text: Within an SST app, resources lacking a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly with raw Pulumi resources and deployed as part of the same app, because SST constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
verdicts.evidence: The official SST config docs say the run function "is where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components," and that "you can add Pulumi code in the run function." The SST Providers docs add that "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers," so raw Pulumi resources deploy as part of the same app.
verdicts.framing_note: The SST docs describe mixing SST and Pulumi components in run(), which covers the claim's special case of resources that have no SST construct. The 'compile to Pulumi resources' reasoning fits SST's documented Pulumi foundation, and a third-party source says each component maps to Pulumi resources.

verdicts.text: SST is not being abandoned; releases continue and the team's attention to opencode hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: Releases do continue: the anomalyco/sst releases page shows v4.17.0 as latest, released 26 Jun 2026. But third-party sources say the opencode shift did change SST's pace. Northflank says "SST's GitHub activity dropped" and "active development shifted to OpenCode" (maintenance mode), and bex.co describes SST as "in maintenance mode since 2025: critical fixes still ship." That contradicts "hasn't changed SST's release cadence." The Pulumi-engine dependency part wasn't disputed.
verdicts.framing_note: "Not abandoned / releases continue" holds up; "release cadence unchanged" goes against sources describing maintenance mode and less activity.
verdicts.intuition_flag: As of Sep 28, 2026, the latest SST release (v4.17.0, June 26) is 3+ months old, which suggests a slower cadence. The two sources describing maintenance mode are a competitor (Northflank) and a blog, so the author should reword or soften the cadence claim rather than assert it.

verdicts.text: Pulumi features such as Pulumi Cloud, policy as code and components can be used alongside SST without leaving the engine SST already uses.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's config reference does back up the components part: "You can use SST and Pulumi components only in the run function." But SST's state "home" provider "Currently supports AWS, Cloudflare and local," so it has no Pulumi Cloud backend. I found no SST docs showing Pulumi policy packs working inside `sst deploy`. So the components claim holds, but "Pulumi Cloud and policy as code alongside SST without leaving the engine" asserts more than SST documents.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: SST documents using Pulumi components. The claim widens that to Pulumi Cloud and policy as code, but SST stores state only in AWS, Cloudflare or local, and its docs don't mention policy packs.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Using Pulumi Cloud with SST probably means running a separate Pulumi project or using ESC/Insights on their own, not the same SST engine run. The author should say which integration path they mean.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; Pulumi policy as code enables guardrails enforced centrally; Pulumi components enable sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
verdicts.evidence: The linked Pulumi Cloud page exists (content/docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud.md) and supports the claim: "Policy as code enforcement applied centrally to every update" plus a "Cloud resource inventory" and org-level collaboration. The components page says packages with components "become discoverable across the organization and can be consumed by any team". The policy page also mentions "Centralized management via Policy Groups". "Cross-team visibility" is the author's wording for the org and inventory features, not a phrase quoted from the docs.
verdicts.framing_note: Short summaries of capabilities the docs describe in more detail; they add nothing the docs don't support.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The blog links /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, but that path is not among the visible aliases of the policy page (content/docs/discovery-governance/policy/_index.md), so check whether this link resolves.

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own v3 announcement (dated August 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3", notes that "SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation", and describes the new engine as one "that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." Pulumi's case-study page separately says SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: The v3 GA post is dated around August 20, 2024. That fits "mid-2024" only loosely; "late summer 2024" or "August 2024" would be more precise.

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." That confirms the bridged-provider design. No source says in so many words that SST never runs the Terraform CLI or writes Terraform state. The claim follows from how it works, though: the Pulumi engine runs deployments, and the v3 post says state is "stored locally and backed up to S3".
verdicts.framing_note: The source's "Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi" plus Pulumi being the deployment engine implies the claim's "no Terraform CLI or Terraform state". That negative is inferred, not stated outright.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Components are defined using Terraform providers" is slightly loose. SST components are built on Pulumi provider packages (e.g. @pulumi/aws), and those happen to be Terraform-bridged.

verdicts.text: SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure sharing across more than one application on its own.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's docs contradict at least the "infrastructure sharing" part: the Reference Resources page says that for a bucket "created in an SST app or in another stage in the same app, there's a similar static sst.aws.Bucket.get method." It also describes referencing resources "managed by a different team." I found no native SST policy enforcement, so that part holds. Cross-team visibility, likely through the SST Console workspace, was not checked.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a compound negative claim about a competitor. SST offers limited cross-app sharing through static .get() lookups and a team Console, so "doesn't expose" overstates things. It would be more accurate to say SST lacks stack references and policy-as-code.

verdicts.text: A blog post exists at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ titled 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi', telling SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
verdicts.evidence: The post exists in the repo with `title: "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi"`, `draft: false`. It tells the story from the SST team's point of view: "we'll explore why SST moved to Pulumi, what challenges they overcame".
verdicts.framing_note: "From SST's side" is a loose summary. The post was written by Pulumi about the SST team's experience (it embeds an SST video) and was not written by SST.

verdicts.text: - [Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi](/blog/any-terraform-provider/) — the bridge SST and others build on
verdicts.evidence: The link /blog/any-terraform-provider/ resolves to a live Pulumi blog post, and its title matches the link text exactly: "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi". The post says Pulumi "now supports using any Terraform or OpenTofu provider with Pulumi", which fits the link's description as the bridge others build on.
verdicts.framing_note: The link text is the post's own title. The note "the bridge SST and others build on" is loose: the post covers Any Terraform Provider (parameterized providers), while SST depends on the wider Pulumi Terraform bridge.
